S2 — THE CRISIS · SOURCED DATA
All stats sourced & cited. Hover any source for full citation. Donut chart: where textile waste goes. Bar chart: fiber production growth. Regulation timeline: EU tailwinds.
The Crisis

Fashion's environmental cost is no longer a footnote

The fashion industry emitted 944 million tonnes of CO₂ in 2023 — a 7.5% spike driven by overproduction and polyester. It consumes 215 trillion litres of water annually, sends 92 million tonnes of textiles to landfill, and loses $150 billion in unrecovered material value every year. Less than 1% of clothing is recycled into new garments.

Regulatory Tailwinds

A wave of EU regulation is creating massive demand for exactly the solutions FIBRA ventures will build — supply chain traceability, circular design, material passports, and producer responsibility systems. LatAm brands exporting to Europe need these capabilities now.

2027
Textile EPR
All EU member states must have textile Extended Producer Responsibility schemes. Brands pay for collection, sorting, and recycling.
2027–28
Digital Product Passport
Every garment sold in the EU needs a QR-linked digital passport with materials, manufacturing, and environmental data.
2028
ESPR Textiles
Mandatory durability, recyclability, and recycled content standards. Ban on destruction of unsold clothing and footwear.
2029
CSDDD
Large brands must identify, prevent, and address human rights and environmental impacts across fashion supply chains.
Source: Carbonfact EU Regulations Overview, 2026

S4 — THE WHITE SPACE
Visual "gap" diagram. Right column items now reference specific EU regulations from the data layer.
The White Space

Latin America has the talent. It lacks the infrastructure.

Fashion accelerators exist in Europe and North America. LatAm sustainable fashion ventures exist in isolation. No program connects them to capital, mentorship, and markets at regional scale — while a wave of EU regulation creates urgent demand for the solutions they're building.

What Exists

  • Circular fashion founders in every country
  • Bio-material innovation (pineapple fiber, cacao, recycled textiles)
  • Artisan heritage and indigenous textile traditions
  • Women-majority textile workforce seeking formalization
  • EU Digital Product Passport mandate from 2027 creating export demand
→

What's Missing

  • Pan-regional acceleration infrastructure
  • Fashion-specific investor pipeline for LatAm
  • Gender-lens M&E framework for fashion ventures
  • Bridge from artisan production to formal markets
  • EU compliance readiness for LatAm brands (ESPR, EPR, DPP)
FIBRA fills this gap.
The first pan-regional, impact-focused fashion accelerator in Latin America.
The Talent

The founders already building the future of fashion

These ventures are in the REIN Hubs pipeline today. FIBRA will accelerate the next generation alongside them.

Track 1 · Circular & Sustainable Fashion

REEMADE SAS

Founded by Ximena Vélez Robledo · Medellín, Colombia

Circular design studio upcycling hard-to-recycle materials — truck tarps, tires, industrial textiles, and coffee waste — into luxury-grade fashion accessories. Their Biomera collection debuted at Colombiamoda 2026.

B2B + Consumer · Circular Manufacturing
Track 2 · Textile Innovation

Green Leaf Natural Fibers

Co-Founded by Jennifer González · Santander, Colombia (est. 2021)

Transforms pineapple crop waste into plant-based textile fibers for fashion, construction, and design. Bridges agricultural waste reduction, rural women's employment, and bio-material innovation.

Bio-materials · Rural Women · Agri-Waste Upcycling
Track 2 · Textile Innovation

Green Leaf — From Field to Fiber

Pineapple leaf harvesting · Santander, Colombia

Workers harvest pineapple leaves that would otherwise be burned or left to rot. Each hectare of pineapple generates 40 tonnes of leaf waste annually — Green Leaf turns this into textile-grade fiber, creating rural employment in the process.

Supply Chain Origin · Job Creation · Zero Waste Agriculture
Track 2 · Textile Innovation

Green Leaf — The Product

Pineapple fiber yarn · Ready for weaving

Raw pineapple leaf fiber processed into yarn spools ready for the textile industry. This is what EU Digital Product Passport-ready, fully traceable material looks like — from field to fabric, every step documented.

DPP-Ready · Traceable · Natural Fiber
Track 2 · Textile Innovation

Green Leaf — Finished Fabric

Woven pineapple fiber textile · Market-ready

The finished product: woven pineapple fiber fabric with a natural linen-like texture. Suitable for fashion, interiors, and accessories. This is the kind of innovation that FIBRA will bring to market at scale.

Market-Ready · Fashion-Grade · Sustainable Textile
S5 — THE PROGRAM
Track cards with hover. Timeline with animated dots. Each track links to a real REIN-pipeline venture.
The Program

Four tracks. Ten ventures. Five countries.

A 16-week acceleration cohort launching Q1 2027, delivered through REIN Hubs' infrastructure across Colombia, Peru, Guatemala, Costa Rica, and El Salvador.

01
Circular & Sustainable Fashion
Circular economy models, regenerative materials, waste-to-product manufacturing, closed-loop design systems.
↳ Example: REEMADE SAS (Colombia) — Upcycling industrial waste into fashion products
02
Textile Innovation
Bio-materials, plant-based fibers, supply chain technology, EU compliance readiness for emerging brands.
↳ Example: Green Leaf (Colombia) — Pineapple waste to textile fiber
03
Artisan Heritage to Market
Formalising indigenous and craft-based businesses, connecting traditional techniques to contemporary markets.
↳ Example: Sourcing from 5 countries with distinct artisan traditions
04
Supply Chain Transparency
Traceability platforms, ethical sourcing verification, B2B SaaS for fashion supply chain management.
↳ Example: TR Global / SLOW (Colombia) — Textile waste management & sorting
